speaker: Boris Cherny
title: Head of Claude Code: What happens after coding is solved | Boris Cherny
question: In AI product development, why do rigid step-by-step workflows and heavy scaffolding around a model often underperform simpler tool-based designs?
guest: One principle is don't try to box the model in. A lot of people's instinct when they build on a model is to layer very strict workflows on it—saying you must do step one, step two, step three with a fancy orchestrator. Almost always you get better results if you just give the model tools, give it a goal, and let it figure it out. Don't try to over-curate it or give it a bunch of context up front; give it a tool so it can get the context it needs. A more general version of this is the bitter lesson: always bet on the more general model over the long term. Rigid workflows put scaffolding around the model, and in general scaffolding might improve performance ten or twenty percent, but those gains often get wiped out with the next model. From the very beginning, we bet on building for the model six months from now, not for the model of today. It's uncomfortable because your product-market fit won't be great at first, but when that model comes out, you hit the ground running.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Rigid workflows encode the developer's assumptions about how a task should be solved, and those assumptions become the ceiling on performance. A hard-coded sequence of steps works only for the cases its designer anticipated; real inputs vary, and when a task deviates, the pipeline can't adapt, backtrack, or skip unnecessary steps. A model given good tools and a clear goal can instead decide what to do based on what it actually observes at each step, recovering from errors and handling novel cases.

Heavy scaffolding also ages badly. Much of it is built to compensate for the weaknesses of a specific model generation, such as poor planning or limited context. As models improve, those crutches turn into constraints: they prevent the model from using its stronger reasoning, and each extra layer adds latency, cost, compounding failure points, and maintenance burden. This is the "bitter lesson" applied to products: general capability tends to beat hand-engineered structure over time.

Rigid workflows still make sense when tasks are narrow, predictable, and demand consistency or auditability. But for open-ended problems, simple, well-designed tools plus model judgment usually generalise better and improve automatically with each model upgrade.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Rigid workflows and heavy scaffolding encode fixed human assumptions about how a task should unfold, constraining the flexible, context-aware reasoning that makes modern models useful. Because real-world inputs rarely follow a predictable happy path, predefined pipelines break on edge cases and prevent the model from dynamically adapting, reprioritizing, or backtracking when an intermediate step fails. Splitting execution across rigid stages and custom sub-prompts also fragments context, creating information bottlenecks where small early errors or lossy summaries compound downstream without a way to self-correct. Simpler tool-based designs—giving the model a clear objective, shared context, and well-defined tools inside an iterative loop—let it inspect actual environment feedback, verify its own work, and recover from mistakes directly. Finally, heavy scaffolding ages poorly: brittle heuristics built to compensate for older model limitations end up capping performance as models improve, adding latency, cost, and maintenance overhead while fighting planning and tool-use capabilities that newer models handle natively.

noweb.answer:
Rigid step-by-step workflows hardcode human assumptions about how a task must unfold, stripping away the adaptability that makes language models valuable. When developers force work through predetermined stages, narrow sub-prompts, and brittle routing logic, context fragments across handoffs and early classification or parsing mistakes cascade without a way to backtrack. Whenever messy real-world inputs deviate from the anticipated happy path, the pipeline breaks.

Simpler tool-based designs perform better because they let the model reason over full context in a closed feedback loop. Given a clear objective, sensible guardrails, and well-defined tools, a model can inspect intermediate results, adjust its strategy on the fly, and recover from errors directly. Heavy scaffolding also ages poorly: intricate glue code and state machines are usually built to patch yesterday’s model weaknesses, turning into maintenance debt and an artificial performance ceiling as models improve. Replacing prescriptive control flow with simple tools reduces latency and compounding failure modes while allowing stronger models to immediately translate into a better product.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Rigid workflows and heavy scaffolding tend to lose because they encode the developer's assumptions about how a task should be solved, and those assumptions age badly as models improve. A hand-built pipeline (classify, then retrieve, then summarize, then verify) caps the system at the designer's foresight. It can't adapt when a task doesn't fit the script, and errors compound across brittle handoffs, since each stage sees only a narrow slice of context. Simpler designs give a capable model a small set of well-documented tools and let it decide what to call, in what order, and when to stop. That uses the model's own reasoning, recovery from mistakes, and judgment about context, which keep getting better with each model generation. This is Rich Sutton's "bitter lesson" applied to products: general methods that scale with capability beat clever hand-engineering. Scaffolding built to work around last year's weaknesses becomes dead weight or an active constraint, and it costs ongoing maintenance. Anthropic's "Building Effective Agents" guidance makes the same point: start simple, and add structure only where it measurably helps, such as for reliability, cost, or compliance.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Rigid step-by-step workflows and heavy scaffolding bake fixed developer assumptions into every transition, making systems brittle whenever real-world inputs are ambiguous, messy, or outside anticipated paths. Breaking a task into many narrow, chained prompts also fragments context and compounds small errors across handoffs, preventing the model from recognizing when an earlier step went wrong or adapting its strategy. By contrast, simpler tool-based designs give the model clear objectives, well-defined tools, and direct feedback from the environment. This lets the model reason end-to-end, choose actions dynamically, and self-correct as new information emerges. Heavy orchestration also tends to become technical debt as foundation models improve: workarounds built to compensate for yesterday’s limitations often constrain stronger models rather than helping them. Lightweight tool-based architectures are not only easier to build, evaluate, and maintain, they also scale naturally with model progress, turning better reasoning directly into better product performance.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Rigid workflows bake in assumptions about what the model will find and what it should do next. When an intermediate result is ambiguous, a tool fails, or the user’s request takes an unexpected turn, the pipeline may keep following the script and compound the error. Heavy scaffolding can also add model calls, handoffs that lose context, and rules that become harder to maintain as models improve.

A simpler tool-based design gives the model a clear goal, a small set of well-defined tools, and feedback from each call. The model can use that feedback to choose the next step, retry, ask for clarification, or stop when it has enough information. Fixed workflows still work well when the steps are predictable or must be enforced. The practical split is to enforce hard requirements in code and let the model make decisions that depend on what it discovers.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Rigid workflows force the model to follow a sequence chosen before it sees the problem. That works when the steps are predictable. When a tool returns an unexpected result, though, the next scripted step may no longer make sense. Each extra handoff can also discard context or turn a mistaken assumption into the starting point for the next step.

A clear goal and a few well-designed tools let the model use what it learns to decide what to do next. It can skip an unnecessary search, ask for missing information, or check a surprising result before acting on it. This also lets a product benefit from improvements in the model without rewriting a workflow built around its earlier limitations. Explicit controls still matter where the product needs guarantees, such as enforcing permissions or validating an action before execution.
